hook: The best AppSec story of the quarter.
voice.lede: One of the strongest B2B AppSec case studies this quarter, arranged in the wrong order. The Rubrik story has a named company, a named executive and real numbers, a 24-hour SLA and 187 compromised npm packages cleared in 30 minutes. The ad body mentions none of it and turns every hard number into a soft adjective, so “tight SLAs” replaces “24-hour SLA.” The operator quote that would stop the scroll sits unused.

findings.title: The raw material is elite
findings.what: A named customer (Rubrik), a named executive, and hard numbers: a 24-hour SLA and 187 compromised npm packages cleared in 30 minutes. This is the kind of proof most B2B ads never get to use.

findings.title: The creative names the outcome
findings.what: “How Rubrik hits aggressive remediation SLAs” is clear and specific, and the two logos side by side do real work. It is the sharpest line in the ad, and it still stops short of the number.

findings.title: Every hard number turned into a soft adjective
findings.what: The ad body turns the real figures into mush, “tight SLAs” instead of “24-hour SLA,” and leaves the operator quote that would stop the scroll completely unused. The strongest assets are in the story but not in the ad.
findings.fix: Lead with the numbers and the quote: 187 packages in 30 minutes, the named exec's words, verbatim. Let the proof do the work it was built for.

findings.title: The page keeps the promise
findings.what: Same customer, same SLA story, and Rubrik’s Head of Security quoted right at the top. A reader who clicked for proof finds it immediately.

findings.title: The key results have no numbers
findings.what: The results box says “rapid response to malware” and “faster remediation.” The 187 packages, the 30 minutes and the 24-hour SLA sit further down, inside the story.
findings.fix: Put the numbers in the results box. It is the first thing a skimming security leader reads.

findings.title: A story ends in two different asks
findings.what: “Book a Demo” and “Start Free Trial” both sit in the header, a bigger ask than the “Learn more” in the ad, and the reader has no single next step that fits having just read a customer story.
findings.fix: Pick one action and put it at the end of the story, where the proof has already done its work.

faq.a: The material behind it is elite, a named customer, a named exec and real numbers. The verdict is “out of order” because the ad buries all of it: it turns hard figures into soft adjectives and leaves the best quote unused, so the strongest AppSec story of the quarter never actually shows up in the ad.

faq.q: What is actually wrong with it?
faq.a: Sequencing. “24-hour SLA” becomes “tight SLAs,” “187 packages cleared in 30 minutes” goes missing, and the operator quote that would stop a scroll sits unused. The assets exist; they are just not the first thing the reader sees.
Put the proof first. Lead the ad with the hardest number (187 packages in 30 minutes) and the named exec's quote, verbatim. The case study is strong enough to carry the ad if you stop softening it.

faq.q: How do I check my own ad for this?
faq.a: Look at your best customer story and your ad side by side: did the real numbers and the real quote make it into the ad, or did they get softened into adjectives? Burying your strongest proof is the most expensive edit you can make. AdRoast scores this automatically, and the first roast is free.

scorecard.label: Headline Clarity
scorecard.note: Creative headline 'How Rubrik hits aggressive remediation SLAs' is clear and specific, though 'one ticket, one fix dream' in body copy is vaguer jargon.

scorecard.label: CTA Friction
scorecard.note: Learn More fits a customer story, but the landing page immediately pushes Book Demo and Start Free Trial, a bigger ask than the ad implied.

scorecard.label: Visual-Copy Match
scorecard.note: Rubrik and Endor logos paired cleanly, gradient text on dark background is on-brand and readable, subhead on creative matches ad body tone.

scorecard.label: Benefit Specificity
scorecard.note: FedRAMP authorization and single pane of glass are concrete, but 'one ticket, one fix dream' undersells the actual reachability-analysis mechanism.

scorecard.label: Trust Signals
scorecard.note: Named customer Rubrik and the FedRAMP claim are strong, specific credibility markers for this buyer, and the page adds a quoted Head of Security.
